notes.meaning: The seventh month was the start of the civil new year, falling in the quiet season between harvest and planting. God called His people to stop their regular work and gather as trumpets were sounded to prepare their hearts for the sacred events of that month. Because they had more free time from daily work, they were encouraged to spend more of it worshiping God.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: A popular modern view teaches that the blowing of trumpets on this day pictures the rapture, when believers will be taken up to meet Christ in the air before the end times.

notes.meaning: The people were told to offer one young bull, one ram, and seven yearling male lambs completely burned on the altar, showing total devotion to the Lord. Each animal had to be healthy and without any physical flaw. Fine flour mixed with olive oil was offered alongside each animal as a grain offering to thank God for providing their daily food.

The priests also had to sacrifice one male goat as a sin offering to make atonement, which means to restore peace between a holy God and sinful people. Even on a joyful holy day, the people needed cleansing so their worship would be acceptable.

These festival sacrifices did not replace the normal morning and evening offerings or the monthly new moon offerings. Special celebrations were added on top of regular devotions rather than pushing them aside.

On the tenth day of the seventh month, Israel held the Day of Atonement, their most solemn day of the year. The people were commanded to stop all work and humble their souls, which meant fasting and sorrowing over their sins before God.

Along with their fasting, the congregation brought a burnt offering of one bull, one ram, and seven lambs, all without defect. These sacrifices were presented with precise portions of flour and oil to honor God's majesty and express total dedication to Him.

A male goat was sacrificed as an extra sin offering on top of the special atonement sacrifices described in Leviticus. This taught Israel that even their prayers, tears, and repentance were imperfect and needed God's cleansing mercy.

On the fifteenth day, Israel began the Feast of Tabernacles, a week-long celebration of thanksgiving after the fruit and grain harvests. The people lived in temporary shelters to remember how God cared for their ancestors in the wilderness for forty years.

The first day of this feast required a massive burnt offering of thirteen young bulls, two rams, and fourteen lambs. Because the harvest had filled their storehouses, the people were called to express their joy through generous giving to the Lord.

A male goat was offered for sin alongside the burnt offerings, and the daily morning and evening lambs were still sacrificed. No amount of rejoicing or public celebration excused the people from dealing with sin or keeping up their regular daily devotions.

On the second day, the offering was the same except that the number of bulls dropped from thirteen to twelve. This steady decrease showed that God gave careful instructions for each day, teaching the people to follow His worship with exact obedience.

On the third day, eleven bulls were offered with the two rams, fourteen lambs, and the daily sin offering. Repeating these sacrifices day after day reminded Israel that God welcomes sincere and steady worship that does not tire of honoring Him.

On the fourth day, ten bulls were sacrificed along with the appointed rams, lambs, grain, and drink offerings. The daily sin offering was still required, pointing out that joy cannot be separated from a clean conscience before God.

On the fifth day, nine bulls were offered following the exact rules God had given. God gradually lightened the cost of the animals as the week went on, showing care for His people while still keeping His altar supplied with worship.

On the sixth day, the priests presented eight bulls, two rams, fourteen lambs, and a male goat. Even as the feast drew toward its close, the people continued to praise God for His protection and the rich fruit of their land.

On the seventh day, the count reached seven bulls, bringing the total number of bulls offered over the week to seventy. Reaching the number seven, the biblical symbol of completeness, rounded out the week of harvest joy under God's covenant blessing.

The day after the week of booths ended was kept as a special closing assembly with no ordinary work permitted. It brought the entire month of sacred festivals to a peaceful and solemn conclusion in God's presence.

The sacrifices for this eighth day were much smaller, requiring only one bull, one ram, seven lambs, and one goat. By reducing the number to just one bull, God reminded the people not to put their trust in large numbers of animal gifts, pointing instead toward one ultimate sacrifice.

These public offerings were presented on behalf of the whole nation at the scheduled festivals, but they were not the only gifts God accepted. Individuals and families were still encouraged to bring their own personal gifts, promises, and thank-offerings to the Lord.

Moses faithfully delivered all these instructions to the people of Israel just as the Lord had spoken to him. Even though Moses knew he would not enter the promised land himself, he made sure the new generation understood how to worship God properly.
